output.summary: Empiric antibiotic regimens for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults typically combine a third-generation cephalosporin with vancomycin; ampicillin is added when Listeria coverage is indicated (age >50 or immunocompromise). Adjunctive dexamethasone has been shown in randomized controlled trials to reduce mortality and unfavorable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis when administered before or with the first dose of antibiotics (de Gans et al., NEJM 2002). Treatment duration for pneumococcal meningitis is 10–14 days per current guidelines. De-escalation to monotherapy is appropriate once susceptibility data are available.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

clinical_pearls: The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status is present in only 44% of bacterial meningitis cases, but at least two of four symptoms (headache, fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status) are present in 95%
Jolt accentuation of headache (worsening with rapid horizontal rotation of the head) has high sensitivity for meningitis and can be a useful bedside test
S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults, accounting for approximately 50% of cases

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Javier Herrera is a 62-year-old right-handed man with a history of type 2 diabetes, chronic sinusitis, and mild right-sided hearing loss who presents to the emergency department via ambulance with approximately 12 hours of progressively worsening headache, fever, and altered mental status. His wife reports that he came home from work yesterday evening around 5 PM complaining of the worst headache of his life, which was diffuse and throbbing in character. He took ibuprofen 600 mg without relief. Over the ensuing hours, he developed shaking chills and his wife measured a temperature of 102.8°F (39.3°C) at 9 PM. He went to bed early but was restless and moaning throughout the night. By 3 AM, his wife noticed he was confused and not making sense when she tried to talk to him. He was complaining that the bedroom light was too bright and kept his eyes closed. He vomited twice between 3 AM and 5 AM, which was non-bloody and non-bilious. She called 911 at approximately 5:15 AM when she could not fully rouse him and he did not recognize their children. EMS found him febrile at 39.5°C with a heart rate of 122 and blood pressure of 148/82. He was transported emergently. In the ED, he is lethargic, photophobic, and in obvious distress. He is intermittently groaning and reaching for his head. Notably, the patient had been treated for an acute sinusitis exacerbation approximately 10 days ago with a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate, which he completed 3 days prior to this presentation. His wife denies any recent head trauma, seizure activity, rash, ear discharge, or known sick contacts with meningitis. She confirms his immunizations are up to date, though she is uncertain about meningococcal vaccination.
